newsitem.title: USA: U.S. mortgage rates jump in week to mid-July highs.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mortgage rates jump in week to mid-July highs.

text.p: Mortgage rates jumped to their highest levels since mid-July this week as fresh signs of strong economic growth revived inflation fears, the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. said Thursday.
Thirty-year fixed-rate mortgages averaged 8.34 percent for the week ended Sept. 6, up from 8.09 percent last week. Fifteen-year fixed-rate mortgages rose to 7.88 percent from 7.60 percent.
Both rates were the highest since the week ended July 12, when the 30-year rate averaged 8.42 percent and the 15-year rate 7.93 percent.
Adjustable mortgage rates rose to an average of 5.85 percent from 5.75 percent last week.
A year ago, the 30-year rate averaged 7.63 percent, the 15-year 7.16 percent, and the adjustable loan 5.86 percent.
"Indications of strong growth in the economy have helped to boost interest rates this week which may influence the Fed to make a move," Freddie Mac Deputy Chief Economist Frank Nothaft said.
The Fed will decide on Sept. 24 whether to boost interest rates to tighten credit and cool any signs of overheating in the economy.

Freddie Mac said lenders charged an average of 1.7 percent in fees and points on 30-year loans, and 1.4 percent on adjustable loans, unchanged on the week. Charges on 15-year loan edged down to 1.6 percent from 1.7 percent.
Separately, the Mortgage Bankers Association of America said the volume of total mortgage applications rose 9.2 percent in the week ended Aug. 30.
The volume of applications to refinance mortgages rose 7.9 percent in the latest survey week, while applications to purchase mortgages rose 9.5 percent, the trade group said.
